newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New S.African leaders wrestle with arms dilemmas.
newsitem.headline: New S.African leaders wrestle with arms dilemmas.

text.p: South Africa's new rulers came to power in a blaze of high-minded idealism but have been tripped up by the messy world of arms deals.

Angry exchanges last week between President Nelson Mandela and the United States over a proposed arms sale to Syria have highlighted the dilemma facing South Africa as it seeks to use its weapons industry to boost foreign trade and generate jobs.
The arms industry expanded rapidly during the apartheid years as a major pillar in isolated South Africa's campaign against Soviet-backed liberation movements.

It became resourceful in the face of world sanctions, with the result that it was possibly South Africa's most successful manufacturing sector when Mandela's African National Congress took power in April 1994.
Arms exports soared in 1995 to 1.04 billion rand ($220 million) from 614 million rand in 1992, and 50,000 people are employed in about 700 companies in the defence industry.
South Africa's artillery, helicopter airframes and landmine-resistant vehicles are particularly highly regarded around the world.
South African defence companies have entered into 93 joint ventures with companies in 20 countries, including Britain, France, the United States, Germany and Malaysia.

During the apartheid years, cash-strapped South Africa sold weapons without scruple -- it armed both Iran and Iraq during the 1980s Gulf War, while at the same time maintaining close military cooperation with Israel.
Mandela's government tried to change all that, setting up a special morals committee to vet arms sales and ensure no weapons were sold to states at war or which abused human rights.
In 1995 an artillery sale to Turkey was vetoed on these grounds, but last year the committee decided it was acceptable to sell arms to Rwanda. That decision was reversed within weeks.

Last week the arms export issue moved from moral soul-searching to international power broking when news leaked of a proposed three billion rand deal to upgrade Syria's ageing Soviet-built T-72 tanks.
"This would have a decisive effect in the Middle East because that's where the big tank battles always take place," said Bill Sass, a military analyst at the independent Institute for Defence Policy.
He said South Africa and Israel's ally the United States, which threatened to cut off aid to Pretoria if the sale went ahead, needed to sit down calmly and thrash out a modus vivendi on arms sales.
"The South African arms industry after all has all sorts of things that it has available, atomic bombs, or the technology at least, and Rooivalk helicopters...
"The two governments must sit down and talk about where they see the industry going, how do they see it being controlled. It needs to be clarified, otherwise it's going to come up again."
Sass said the South African upgrade for T-72 fire-control was regarded as possibly the best currently available.
If Syria bought it, a potentially huge market would open up because of the tens of thousands of T-72 tanks in former Soviet- supplied countries around the world all needed upgrading.

"Previously Russia would have supplied new tanks but now all those countries have got to stretch the lifespan of the T-72 as long as they can because they can't replace it... (For South Africa), there's a lot of jobs involved," Sass said.
The jobs argument is one frequently raised by Armscor, the state weapons agency, which has struggled to throw off its image as a creation and servant of apartheid.

"I think there's a majority view now that the arms industry is an important part of the economy," said Abba Omar, a former ANC activist who is now communications chief at Armscor. "Opposition to it has declined, but we do need control measures."
The latest moral broadside against the arms industry was fired on Sunday by the Archbishop of Cape Town, Njongonkulu Ndungane, who wrote in a newspaper:
"By exporting arms, all we are doing is selling the hardware of an industry which is historically the fruit of the sanctions- busting apartheid years...
"The South African government has a responsibility to its peace-loving citizens to scrap arms sales, for short-term gain, to any country." $=4.6 rand
